title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Window cleaning (all heights)
audience: Window cleaning owners and team leads who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a window need may be starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what window work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the window jobs you do well, the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A regular round of exterior and track cleans on a route you already run is worth more to a small business than a single large job across town. The Oneflare sample of a monthly job for 15 or more windows is one marketplace listing, not evidence of demand in your area, so test the repeat need in your own suburbs.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list, and be plain about the evidence
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using written criteria: service area, repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the job falls within your licence and insurance. Candidate segments include property managers, strata managers, real-estate offices, owners corporation committees and holiday rental managers. This research found no evidence that window cleaners buy from strata managers or real-estate offices, and no gutter-schedule evidence at all. The Consumer Victoria page says an owners corporation manages common property and raises fees to pay for it, but it does not mention windows and does not say whether external windows are common property; that depends on the plan of subdivision. Treat each candidate segment as one to test, not one that has been proven. Add a prospect only when it passes the criteria, and record the date and source of its contact details. Use only contact details published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested lists.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals, and use them for timing only
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples are a planning application for alterations at a multi-unit site in one of your suburbs, a new business on a street where you already work, or a change of occupier at a site you already service. The City of Casey planning permit register on Victoria's open data portal shows application status and suburb. Check your own council's register, since each council publishes its own. Building permit data records location, estimated cost and issue date, and can be filtered by suburb, but it does not show whether a window cleaning need follows; use it for area planning, not for contacting individuals. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts. No window-cleaning tender was found in this research, so check the portal for any that appear. Do not monitor private people, do not enter common property without an invitation, and do not go to a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you learned of the notice or the business, makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or the business's own material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for the street-facing windows of one building. Keep it short and do not overstate what you know. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling says many approaches were pressured or misleading, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. A specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage. Where the message goes by email or text, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, then a pause. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the window job, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and the source of its contact details.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as a council planning register and tender alerts, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and your licence and insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A window cleaner covers three suburbs. A planning register entry shows an application for alterations at a three-storey building in one suburb, and the body corporate manager's business email address is published on the building's contact page.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA's guidance says that publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the owner first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the manager has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the owner checks the register before calling. Any message that does go out names the application, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific item the business could handle, and asks one question. The owner does not contact individual owners or tenants using private details, and does not enter the building without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Offering window work at a height or access method you are not licensed or insured for.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. No licence for window cleaning was found in this research, apart from the NSW high-risk work licence for large boom platforms. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check each one you work in. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Public information does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is unconfirmed here, so check the OAIC's small-business guidance. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the window work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals for timing, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked. Strata and real-estate prospects are untested for window work.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which window prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A planning register shows alterations at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for window cleaning
Go into the common area to look at the windows before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a window prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include a free unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some others. The page as read lists the APP chapters only; small-business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: OAIC.
